lede: From the accession of Selim II to the loss of La Goleta, and then the long afterlife in print. Dates follow the documents carried here; where modern accounts differ, the entry says so.

stations.text: The new sultan inherits Sokollu Mehmed Pasha as grand vizier. Cyprus, a Venetian island between Anatolia, Syria and Egypt, lies inside the Ottoman sea.

An Ottoman envoy demands the island; Venice refuses. Malim sets out both titles to the island: Venice's by the adoption of Caterina Cornaro, Selim's 'in the right of the Soldan of Ægypt'. In Istanbul the Şeyhülislam Ebussuud rules that a peace with the infidels may be broken when breaking it serves the Muslims better.
Lala Mustafa Pasha lands on the island with the army that will take both its fortresses; Piyale Pasha, who outranks him, carries his tent ashore.
The capital is stormed after a seven-week siege. A Christian relief fleet, gathered too late and divided in its command, turns back that autumn.
A Venetian squadron runs men and supplies into the last fortress; 'the sixteenth day of February' it sails again, leaving about four thousand foot and eight hundred picked soldiers.

Pius V, Philip II and Venice conclude the league in Rome; the copy printed by Dumont dates its publication in consistory 26 May. Two hundred galleys, the cost in sixths, and the Pope as judge of every quarrel. In London a year later Malim prays for 'the covenant the Christian monarchs have struck'.
Mines, batteries and six general assaults, repulsed one by one while the powder runs down to seven barrels.

stations.titel: Surrender, and the killing of the commanders
stations.text: Famagusta surrenders on terms. In Mustafa's tent the commanders are seized and killed; Bragadin is mutilated and later flayed alive. Martinengo, the report's author, sells himself as a slave to save his life. Martinengo dates the handing over to 15 August; modern accounts put the surrender at the start of the month and Bragadin's death on the 17th. Peçevî, after Mustafa Âlî, tells the same scene from the Ottoman side, with a reason Martinengo denies: the Muslim captives killed on the night of the surrender (Peç. Cyprus [12]).
Don John of Austria arrives in Messina and joins the Venetian and papal squadrons; the combined fleet sails in mid-September.

At the mouth of the Gulf of Patras the League's fleet destroys the Ottoman fleet of Müezzinzade Ali Pasha. Uluç Ali escapes with his squadron. Cervantes is wounded; the captive of his novel is taken prisoner. From the Ottoman side, Peçevî: the fleet sent out short of men, its commander bound by orders from Istanbul, and no such defeat 'since Noah invented the ship'. Kâtip Çelebi (1656) adds the Bloody Cape and a moral: commanders should not fight at sea as on land.

Under Sokollu and Uluç Ali, now Kılıç Ali Pasha, the Ottoman arsenal builds a new fleet in a single winter, with eight new slipways laid out in the Sultan's garden. More than two hundred galleys are ready before the spring.

stations.titel: Malim's translation; the death of Pius V
stations.text: Malim dates his dedication from Lambeth, 23 March 1572. Pius V dies on 1 May; he had instituted a feast of Our Lady of Victory for the anniversary of the battle.

The League's second campaign finds the Ottoman fleet in harbour and fails to bring it to battle. 'There I saw and observed how the opportunity … was lost.' From the Ottoman side, Kılıç Ali declines battle because 'the eye of the army of Islam is frightened' and shelters under the guns of Modon (Tuhfe 1572–73 [1]).

Venice gives up Cyprus and pays an indemnity, against the article that no confederate may treat with the Turk without the others' consent. 'He made peace with the Venetians (who were much more eager for it than he was).' Kâtip Çelebi records it as an order to the fleet at sea: spare the lands of Venice, lay waste those of Spain (Tuhfe 1572–73 [2]).
A Spanish success without the League, and a short-lived one.
The Ottoman fleet takes La Goleta and the new fort at Tunis. The captive at the oar: 'as if to make that eternal … these stones were needed to support it.'
The King of Scots prints his heroic poem on the battle; reprinted in London in 1603 as 'His Majesties Lepanto'. (Named, not yet carried.)
The captive's tale in Part I; in the prologue to Part II Cervantes defends the hand lost 'on the grandest occasion the past or present has seen'.
The crusading ballad that fixed the battle in English memory, a year before the Balkan wars.
